By Grace Crivellaro

Topic:Missing Person

Thu 11 Jun 2026 at 12:30pm

Thu 11 Jun 2026 at 6:02pm

Kevin Docherty reading out an opening submission at the inquiry into missing persons, alongside retired police officer Jeff Dakers.  (ABC News)

An inquiry has heard from the brothers of Cheryl Grimmer, a three-year-old who was kidnapped from Fairy Meadow Beach in Wollongong, New South Wales, in January 1970.

It also heard from the twin brother of Kay Docherty, who went missing when she was aged 16 in 1979. He believes her disappearance could be linked to notorious killer Ivan Milat.

The inquiry continues in Grafton in July.

Relatives of missing people have detailed police failures and demanded accountability decades on from the disappearance of their loved ones, some of which are believed to be linked to the notorious Australian serial killer, Ivan Milat.

Their grief and frustrations were aired during the first hearing of a NSW parliamentary inquiry into unsolved murders and long-term missing persons' cases, which sat in Bowral on Thursday.

Ricki Nash, the brother of three-year-old Cheryl Grimmer, who was kidnapped from Fairy Meadow beach in Wollongong in 1970, called for transparency from authorities about what they knew about her disappearance at the time.

Paul Grimmer and Ricki Nash address a press conference about their missing sister, Cheryl Grimmer, in 2025. (ABC Illawarra: Kelly Fuller)

He said his family would have known what happened long ago if police had done their job, believing vital leads were not followed.

The inquiry heard a 17-year-old boy, known under the pseudonym Mercury for legal reasons, made a graphic confession claiming responsibility for the toddler’s murder.

"Yet despite the seriousness of that confession, my parents were never told," Mr Nash said.

"How is it possible that such a detailed confession sat gathering dust in the archives for more than 45 years?

"Why was Mercury never re-interviewed and challenged about how he knew the details he described in his confession?"

Cheryl Grimmer, shown with her father and on Fairy Meadow Beach. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Mr Nash also questioned why police publicised a ransom note asking for $10,000 two days before the money was due to be collected, saying what should have been a controlled ordeal had instead been a "public spectacle".

"The author demanded a pardon, terminology far more common in England than Australia. Mercury himself was a recent immigrant from England," Mr Nash said.

"Those connections deserved to be thoroughly investigated and were not during the 2011 coronial inquest 41 years later."

Mercury was charged over Cheryl's murder in 2017, but the trial collapsed due to his confession being ruled  inadmissible due to more recent laws requiring a minor be accompanied by a support person when interviewed by police.

The inquiry heard the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions was reviewing its decision to discontinue its case against Mercury.

Cheryl Grimmer's disappearance is the oldest cold case being handled by the Unsolved Homicide Squad.

Kevin Docherty told the inquiry of how police knocked on his door in 1979 to tell his family his 15-year-old twin sister, Kay, was missing after she disappeared from Warilla, south of Wollongong.

Kay was last seen near a bus stop on Shellharbour Road and may have been hitchhiking with her friend Toni Cavanagh.

Cheryl Grimmer, Kay Docherty and Toni Cavanagh, three of the many people whose cases will fall within the scope of the new parliamentary inquiry.  (Supplied)

In 2013, an inquest found Kay and Toni likely died shortly after their disappearance and that there was evidence to suggest Ivan Milat may have murdered them.

Thirty years after their disappearance, Mr Docherty said detectives arrived at his family's home to tell them they were investigating Kay's cold case.

"This was the first contact [from police] in 30 years," Mr Docherty told the inquiry.

Since 2020, Mr Docherty said he, retired police officer Jeff Dakers, and Search Dogs Sydney  scoured an area of scrubland on the border of Primbee and Windang where Milat was reportedly seen.

They believe Kay's body could be buried in an overgrown site and have suggested controlled burns to gain access to the spot where a witness said Milat chased him.

The centre has allowed Kevin Docherty to share his experience with other families. (ABC Illawarra: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

Mr Dakers told the inquiry that, alongside Mr Doherty, he had been unable to obtain permission from Illawarra detectives to clear the land off Bakers Lane for a search.

"Police cannot have the excuse that we don't have the resources; we've got many volunteers who would love to go and assist," he said.

"I've had all the excuses. All I'm doing is hitting brick walls all the way along with everything I'm doing."

Mr Docherty's account is one of dozens of public submissions before the inquiry possibly linked to Milat.

Between 1989 and 1992, Milat abducted, assaulted, and murdered five foreign backpackers and two Australian tourists, dumping their bodies in Belanglo State Forest.

He was sentenced to seven consecutive life terms in 1996 and died from cancer in prison in October 2019.

NSW MLC Jeremy Buckingham, who is chairing the inquiry, said the inquiry had received "scores" of reports of assaults or near-misses that were only later associated with Milat.

The inquiry also heard from the family of Keren Rowland, who was 20 years old when she went missing in 1971.

They detailed a swathe of alleged police failures, including the loss of several pieces of evidence.

Her family believes she may have been one of Milat’s first victims, and that if authorities connected him to her disappearance, his targeting of backpackers may have been prevented.

The inquiry will resume in Grafton in July.
